# Propositional Logic {#sec-propositional-logic .chapter}

## Introduction {#sec-propositional-logic-introduction}

Propositional logic is the study of the inferential relations that obtain between compound propositions that are built up from other more simple propositions through the application of various logical operations.
The specific system of propositional logic that we will study in this chapter will focus on a particular kind of proposition forming operation, namely, that which yields a compound proposition the truth value of which is a function of the truth values of the component propositions from which it is constructed.
Such operations are all called 'truth-functional' operations, or, 'Boolean' operations, for short.[^Boole]

[^Boole]: The label 'Boolean' is in honor of the English mathematician George Boole, whose seminal work, _An Investigation of the Laws of Thought_ [-@Boole1854-ur], layed the foundation for the branch of mathematics now called Boolean algebra.
In the examples given in this chapter, we will explain, in more detail, how Boolean algebra can be view as a system of propositional logic.

Truth-functional, or Boolean, propositional logic forms the core of most other systems of logic utilized in philosophical analysis, including first-order predicate logic and modal logic.[^classical] It also provides the standard context in which the theory of probability is developed.
It thus constitutes the first essential entry in a philosophy student's logical toolkit.

In this chapter, we will introduce a formal language in which to represent arguments of propositional logic, a semantic framework in which to assess their validity, and a deductive system in which to carry out proofs.
We will then proceed to show that this deductive system is both sound and complete.

[^classical]: Truth-functional, or Boolean, propositional logic is often referred to as _classical_ propositional logic.
This label is a misnomer, for truth-functional propositional logic is neither classical in the sense of being the first system of propositional logic to have been studied, nor in the sense of having its origin in Greek or Latin antiquity.
The use of the label 'classical' to describe truth-functional propositional logic seems to have gained widespread usage in the mid-20th century, mainly to distinguish truth-functional propositional logic from the alternative intuitionistic, relevantistic and other non-classical systems of propositional logic that began to be studied more widely at that time.

## The Syntax and Semantics of Propositional Logic {#sec-propositional-logic-the-syntax-and-semantics-of-propositional-logic}

### The Language $\Lp$

We begin by defining a formal language for propositional logic, which we will refer to as $\Lp$.
The alphabet for the language consists, first, of an infinite number of symbols:

$$
  \p_1,\p_2,\ldots,\p_n,\ldots
$$

We refer to these symbols as atoms.
In addition to the atoms, the alphabet also includes four special symbols:

$$
  \neg\hspace{0.05in},\hspace{0.05in} \conj\hspace{0.05in},\hspace{0.05in}
  \disj\hspace{0.05in},\hspace{0.05in} \imp
$$

These are referred to collectively as propositional connectives, and, respectively, as the negation operator ($\neg$), the conjunction operator ($\conj$), the disjunction operator ($\disj$), and the conditional operator ($\imp$).
The latter three connectives (i.e., $\conj, \disj$, and $\imp$) are referred to as binary connectives, whereas the negation operator is referred to as a unary connective.

Lastly, the alphabet for $\Lp$ also includes the left and right parentheses:

$$
(\hspace{0.07in},\hspace{0.07in})
$$

As always, expressions of the language are finite strings of symbols taken from its alphabet.
The sentences of the language are given by the following inductive definition:

:::{#def-sentences-p .definition}

The sentences of $\Lp$ are defined inductively as follows:

1. Any expression consisting of a single atom is a sentence.

2. If $\ph$ is a sentence, then the expression $(\neg \ph)$ is a sentence.

3. If $\ph$ and $\psi$ are sentences and $\ast$ is a binary connective, then the expression $(\ph\ast\psi)$ is a sentence.

:::

Sentences of $\Lp$ include:

i. $\p_7$

ii. $(\neg \p_2)$

iii. $(\p_4 \disj \p_{21})$

iv. $(\neg(\neg \p_{14}))$

v. $((\p_3\imp (\neg \p_3)) \conj (\p_{21}\disj \p_{3}))$

vi. $(\p_{16}\imp(\p_{16}\conj (\p_{16} \imp \p_{16})))$

We refer to those sentences consisting of a single atom as atomic sentences.
The sentence $(\neg \ph)$ is referred to as the negation of $\ph$.
If $\ph$ is either an atomic sentence or the negation of an atomic sentence, we refer to $\ph$ as a literal.
The sentence $(\ph\conj\psi)$ is referred to as the conjunction with left conjunct $\ph$ and right conjunct $\psi$, or simply the conjunction of $\ph$ and $\psi$.
The sentence $(\ph\disj \psi)$ is referred to as the disjunction with left disjunct $\ph$ and right disjunct $\psi$, or simply the disjunction of $\ph$ and $\psi$.
The sentence $(\ph\imp \psi)$ is referred to as the conditional with antecedent $\ph$ and consequent $\psi$.
Conjunctions, disjunctions, and conditionals are referred to, collectively, as binary compounds.

We have not yet shown that the labels negation, conjunction, disjunction, etc., are mutually exclusive.
That is, we have not yet shown that a given sentence cannot, for example, be both a conjunction and a conditional.
Nor have we shown that a sentence which is a conjunction must have unique left and right conjuncts.
We will soon confirm that this is indeed the case, but for now we turn to the task of specifying a semantics for the language.

:::
